title: 401(K) VS BROKERAGE: 6 THINGS TO KNOW
series_label: MAX 401(K) OR BROKERAGE ACCOUNT?: 6 THINGS TO KNOW

concepts.title: The 4-Step Priority List
concepts.body: Order matters. (1) Get the full 401(k) match — that's a 50%-100% instant return. (2) Build a $1,000 emergency fund. (3) Max a Roth IRA ($7,500 in 2026). (4) Go back and max the 401(k) ($24,500). Only after all four should you send extra to a taxable brokerage.

concepts.title: Why Match Comes First
concepts.body: An employer match is a guaranteed return on day one. A 50% match on your 6% contribution is an instant 50% gain before any market movement. No investment in history reliably returns 50% on day one. Leaving match on the table is the most expensive 'savings' mistake.

visual_spec.callout_text: 401(k) match first. A 50% match is a 50% instant return — nothing in the market reliably gives you that. Always contribute enough to get the full match.

concepts.title: 2026 Limits Side By Side
concepts.body: The two accounts have separate caps. 2026 401(k) elective limit: $24,500 ($32,500 at 50+). 2026 Roth IRA limit: $7,500 ($8,600 at 50+). You can max both if you have the earned income — they're not either/or. A $75,000 earner can put $32,000/yr away in tax-advantaged space.

concepts.title: When Brokerage Wins
concepts.body: A taxable brokerage has no contribution limit, no income limit, and no withdrawal penalty. It's flexible in ways IRAs and 401(k)s aren't. The cost: no upfront tax break and capital gains tax on profits. Use it for goals before age 59½ (house down payment, etc.) and overflow savings.

concepts.title: The $75,000 Salary Example
concepts.body: A $75,000 earner who maxes both gets $32,000/yr into tax-advantaged accounts — $24,500 in the 401(k) plus $7,500 in the Roth IRA. Add a 4% employer match ($3,000) and the total is $35,000/yr. A 401(k)-only saver at the same salary is leaving 22% of that tax-advantaged space empty.

concepts.title: A Common Mistake
concepts.body: Don't choose one. The error is treating 'max 401(k)' and 'open brokerage' as competing goals. The real order is: match → emergency fund → Roth IRA → 401(k) max → then brokerage. Skipping the Roth IRA to over-fund a 401(k) is leaving $7,500 of tax-free space on the table every year.

visual_spec.callout_text: It's not 401(k) OR brokerage. It's match → Roth → 401(k) max → brokerage. Skipping the Roth IRA to over-fund a 401(k) is leaving tax-free space unused.

sources_footer: Sourced from IRS IR-2025-111, IRS Publication 590-A, IRS Publication 575, FINRA Smart Investing
